outcome: A single-author arXiv preprint (Owen Root, Aug/Sep 2025) claims to prove that the fractional-part condition 2^k·{(3/2)^k} + ⌊(3/2)^k⌋ > 2^k never occurs, which — combined with prior work of Dickson, Pillai, Rubugunday and Niven — would fix a fully general closed-form expression g(k) = 2^k − ⌊(3/2)^k⌋ − 2 for all k. As of this writing (over a year after posting, two versions, no journal submission or expert digestion found), it has not been checked or accepted by the mathematical community; the only public assessment found is a fully automated ('machine-made') review flagging that the abstract does not even state the condition being proved, making it hard to evaluate even provisionally.
summary: Waring's problem bullet on this list covers two separate open quantities: g(k), for which a conjectural general formula g(k) = 2^k − ⌊(3/2)^k⌋ − 2 has long been known to hold except possibly when a specific fractional-part condition occurs (it is known not to occur for all currently checked k, and never for large k by results of Mahler-type arguments, but not proved impossible for all k), and G(k), for which only bounds are known for k ≥ 7 or so. Searching the window (26 Jan 2024 to present), I found one candidate event: arXiv:2508.17950 by Owen Root (a physics PhD candidate at CUNY, per their alphaXiv profile — not previously known in this subfield), first posted 25 Aug 2025 and revised 4 Sep 2025, titled 'Expression for g(k) Related to Waring's Problem'. Its abstract states it proves the outstanding condition never occurs, which would settle g(k) in closed form for every k — a full resolution of that half of the bullet, not just a case, if correct. However, I found no evidence any human expert has read through and endorsed the argument: no journal listing, no digestion on blogs (Tao's blog, Quanta, etc. — none found), and the one public review is from Pith Review, an explicitly 'machine-made' (automated/LLM) review platform that itself flags the paper as unverifiable from the abstract alone and 'important enough to warrant expert review', i.e. a request for human checking that (as far as I can determine) has not yet happened. Per §6.1 this is squarely 'claimed', not 'resolved': a preprint that no digestion has verified. On the AI question: the paper's own text contains no acknowledgement of AI/ML tool use in producing the proof (checked via full-text fetch of the HTML version), so there is no basis for 'assisted' or 'generated'. The only AI system anywhere in this problem's timeline is Pith's automated reviewer, which only assessed/critiqued the preprint — a checking function, not a mathematics-producing one — so per §6.2 that is 'none', not 'assisted' or 'generated', regardless of how central Pith's critique is to the current epistemic status of the claim. Separately, one of the triage's found items, arXiv:2401.13436 ('Further Improvements on Waring's Problem G(k)' by An-Ping Li), was submitted 21 Jan 2024 — four days before the frozen revision's 26 Jan 2024 timestamp — so it is not an in-window event and is excluded from consideration (it would in any case not involve AI, being a classical exponential-sums/Hardy-Littlewood-circle-method argument). I found no other G(k) bound improvements, small-k value determinations, or g(k) work in the window besides Root's preprint. The Wikipedia article's live lead (checked, though not authoritative for this project) still cites only pre-2003 literature and does not mention Root's or Li's work, consistent with no accepted change yet.
competing_reading: One could argue this should be 'progress' rather than 'claimed', on the theory that an unverified single-author preprint on an open problem with this track record (many false or flawed claimed proofs of number-theoretic closed forms circulate on arXiv) is closer to 'nothing has really moved' than to a live claim awaiting adjudication. I kept it as 'claimed' per §6.1's literal definition ('a preprint, announcement or machine-checked certificate that experts have not yet digested') since the preprint's proof, if it holds up, would be a full resolution of the g(k)-formula question, not a partial bound — that is a meaningfully different situation from a mere incremental bound (which would be 'progress'). Also arguable: whether Pith Review's automated critique itself, being a form of AI-driven mathematical review, deserves separate notice as a 'progress'/'incident'-flavored data point about AI infrastructure entering the peer-review pipeline for this problem; I judged it does not rise to an event about the problem's mathematical status and is better treated as part of the evidentiary picture for 'claimed' vs 'resolved', not as its own event.
what_would_settle_it: A human expert's digestion of arXiv:2508.17950 (blog post, MathSciNet review, or journal referee report) either confirming the proof of the fractional-part condition or identifying an error; alternatively, any independent proof or disproof of that same condition; or any new arXiv preprint on G(k) small-value determinations or asymptotic bounds dated after 26 Jan 2024 that I did not surface.
